questions.explanation: 「あ」 is a. 「お」 (o) is the closest look-alike: it has a separate dot at the top right, which 「あ」 does not.
「お」 is o. The separate dot at the top right is what makes it 「お」. 「あ」 (a) has no dot, and 「む」 (mu) has a dot too, but its stroke ends in a tail to the right.
「い」 is i. 「い」 has two short strokes side by side, the right one shorter. In 「り」 (ri) the right stroke is the long one and sweeps down.
「り」 is ri. In 「り」 the right-hand stroke is long and curves down, while in 「い」 (i) it is the shorter of the two. 「け」 (ke) has a crossing stroke as well.
「さ」 is sa. 「さ」 and 「ち」 (chi) are mirror images of each other, which is why they are so easy to swap. 「き」 (ki) is 「さ」 with a second horizontal stroke.
「ち」 is chi. 「ち」 is the mirror image of 「さ」 (sa): its lower curve bulges to the right, like the bottom of a 5. 「ら」 (ra) starts with a separate dot.
「き」 is ki. Two horizontal strokes make it 「き」; 「さ」 (sa) has only one. 「ま」 (ma) also has two, but it ends in a loop.
「ぬ」 is nu. 「ぬ」 and 「め」 (me) share their shape, but 「ぬ」 finishes with a small loop and 「め」 does not.
「め」 is me. 「め」 has no loop at the end of its long stroke; 「ぬ」 (nu) does. That loop is the only difference worth looking for.
「ね」 is ne. 「ね」, 「れ」 (re) and 「わ」 (wa) share the same left side. 「ね」 ends in a loop, 「れ」 ends with a flick outwards and 「わ」 ends in a round curve.
「れ」 is re. The right side of 「れ」 ends with a flick outwards. With a loop it would be 「ね」 (ne); with a round curve it would be 「わ」 (wa).
「わ」 is wa. 「わ」 ends in a round curve, with no loop like 「ね」 (ne) and no outward flick like 「れ」 (re).
「る」 is ru. 「る」 has a small loop at the bottom; 「ろ」 (ro) is the same shape without it.
「ろ」 is ro. No loop at the bottom makes it 「ろ」. Add one and it becomes 「る」 (ru).
「は」 is ha. 「は」 has one horizontal stroke on its right side; 「ほ」 (ho) has two. As a character it is ha, even though it is read wa when it is a particle.
「ほ」 is ho. 「ほ」 has two horizontal strokes on the right; 「は」 (ha) has one. 「ま」 (ma) has two strokes as well, but no vertical line on the left.
「け」 is ke. 「け」 has a vertical line on the left and a crossing stroke with a long line on the right. 「は」 (ha) ends in a loop that 「け」 does not have.
「に」 is ni. 「に」 is a vertical line followed by two short horizontal strokes. Without the vertical line it would be 「こ」 (ko).
「た」 is ta. 「た」 is a cross with 「こ」 written beside it. 「な」 (na) has a cross too, but ends in a loop.
「な」 is na. 「な」 has a cross, a dot and a loop at the bottom right. 「た」 (ta) has the cross but finishes with two short strokes instead of a loop.
「し」 is shi. 「し」 is a single stroke that goes down and hooks up to the right. 「つ」 (tsu) is a curve on its side, opening to the bottom left.
「つ」 is tsu. 「つ」 is one curved stroke lying on its side. 「う」 (u) has the same curve with a short stroke above it.
「う」 is u. 「う」 is a short stroke above a curve. 「ら」 (ra) also starts with a short stroke, but its second stroke runs down the left before curving.
「す」 is su. 「す」 has a horizontal stroke crossed by a vertical one with a loop in it. 「む」 (mu) has a similar loop but also a dot at the top right.
「む」 is mu. 「む」 has the loop of 「す」 (su) plus a separate dot at the top right, and its stroke ends with a tail running off to the right.
「ん」 is n. 「ん」 looks rather like a handwritten h and is the only basic kana with no vowel. 「そ」 (so) zigzags across instead.

questions.stem: Which hiragana stands for the sound 'nu'?
questions.explanation: nu is written 「ぬ」. 「ぬ」 ends in a small loop. 「め」 (me) is the same shape without it.

questions.stem: Which hiragana stands for the sound 'chi'?
questions.explanation: chi is written 「ち」. 「ち」 curves out to the right like the bottom of a 5. Its mirror image, 「さ」, is sa.

questions.stem: Which hiragana stands for the sound 'ru'?
questions.explanation: ru is written 「る」. The loop at the bottom is the clue: 「る」 has one, 「ろ」 (ro) does not.

questions.stem: Which hiragana stands for the sound 'wa'?
questions.explanation: wa is written 「わ」. 「わ」 ends in a plain round curve. 「ね」 (ne) ends in a loop and 「れ」 (re) in an outward flick.

questions.stem: Which hiragana stands for the sound 'ho'?
questions.explanation: ho is written 「ほ」. 「ほ」 has two horizontal strokes on the right; 「は」 (ha) has one.

questions.stem: Which hiragana stands for the sound 'tsu'?
questions.explanation: tsu is written 「つ」. 「つ」 is a single curve on its side. 「し」 (shi) runs down and hooks up instead, and 「く」 (ku) is a sharp angle like <.

questions.stem: Which hiragana stands for the sound 'ri'?
questions.explanation: ri is written 「り」. In 「り」 the right-hand stroke is the long one. In 「い」 (i) it is the shorter one.

questions.stem: Which hiragana stands for the sound 'ki'?
questions.explanation: ki is written 「き」. 「き」 has two horizontal strokes across the top; 「さ」 (sa) has one, and 「ま」 (ma) ends in a loop.
「が」 is 「か」 (ka) with the two short strokes called dakuten, which voice the sound: k becomes g. Dakuten on 「さ」 would give za, and on 「た」, da.
The small circle, handakuten, turns 「は」 (ha) into 「ぱ」 (pa). The two strokes of dakuten would make it 「ば」 (ba) instead.
「ぶ」 is 「ふ」 (fu) with dakuten, so it is bu. With the small circle it would be 「ぷ」 (pu).
Dakuten turns 「し」 (shi) into 「じ」 (ji). 「ぎ」 (gi) comes from 「き」 instead, and 「ち」 (chi) has no marks at all.
「ど」 is 「と」 (to) with dakuten, so t becomes d. 「ぼ」 (bo) and 「ご」 (go) come from 「ほ」 and 「こ」.
The small circle makes 「ほ」 (ho) into 「ぽ」 (po). Two strokes would give 「ぼ」 (bo), so the circle and the strokes must be looked at carefully.

questions.stem: Which kana do you get by adding the dakuten ゛ to 「さ」?
questions.explanation: Dakuten voices the sound without changing the vowel, so 「さ」 (sa) becomes 「ざ」 (za). 「ぜ」 (ze) comes from 「せ」, and 「だ」 (da) from 「た」.

options: a small つ written after it
questions.explanation: The small circle, handakuten, gives the p sounds: ぱ, ぴ, ぷ, ぺ, ぽ. The two short strokes of dakuten would make 「ば」 (ba).

questions.stem: Which row of hiragana can take the small circle ゜?
options: the か and さ rows
questions.explanation: Handakuten goes only on the は row, giving ぱ, ぴ, ぷ, ぺ and ぽ. The か, さ, た and は rows can all take dakuten, but the circle belongs to one row alone.

questions.stem: Which sound does 「きゃ」 stand for?
questions.explanation: A small 「ゃ」 blends with the kana before it into a single beat: きゃ is kya. Written full size, 「きや」 would be two beats, ki-ya.

questions.stem: Which sound does 「しゅ」 stand for?
questions.explanation: 「し」 plus a small 「ゅ」 blends into shu, one beat. 「しょ」 is sho and 「ちゅ」 is chu.

questions.stem: Which sound does 「ちょ」 stand for?
questions.explanation: 「ち」 plus a small 「ょ」 is cho, as in ちょっと (chotto). Written with a full-size 「よ」, 「ちよ」 would be two beats, chi-yo.

questions.stem: Which sound does 「りょ」 stand for?
questions.explanation: 「り」 with a small 「ょ」 is ryo, as in りょこう (ryokou, travel). 「りゅ」 would be ryu and 「りゃ」 rya.

questions.stem: Which sound does 「じゃ」 stand for?
questions.explanation: 「じ」 with a small 「ゃ」 is ja, as in じゃあね (jaa ne). 「ちゃ」, without dakuten, would be cha.

questions.stem: Which sound does 「にゅ」 stand for?
questions.explanation: 「に」 with a small 「ゅ」 is nyu, one beat, as in ぎゅうにゅう (gyuunyuu, milk). 「ぬ」 on its own is nu, a different kana altogether.

questions.stem: How do you read 「びょういん」?
questions.explanation: 「びょういん」 (byouin) means hospital: the small 「ょ」 blends with 「び」 and the 「う」 makes the o long. With a full-size 「よ」, 「びよういん」 (biyouin) is a hairdresser's, so the size of one kana changes the word.

questions.stem: How do you read 「とうきょう」?
questions.explanation: Tokyo is 「とうきょう」 (toukyou): two long o sounds, each written with 「う」, and a small 「ょ」 blending 「き」 into kyo. The English spelling drops both long vowels.
A small 「っ」 doubles the consonant after it, with a short pause: きって (kitte) means stamp. 「きて」 (kite) is a different word with no pause.

questions.stem: How do you read 「がっこう」?
questions.explanation: The small 「っ」 doubles the k and the 「う」 lengthens the o: gakkou, school. Reading the small 「っ」 as a full tsu gives gatsukou, which is not a word.
Before shi, the small 「っ」 doubles the s: zasshi, magazine. In romaji the small 「っ」 shows up as a doubled letter, so っし is sshi.

questions.stem: What does the small 「っ」 in 「まって」 do?
options: It doubles the t, with a short pause before it
It adds a separate tsu sound before the t
It makes the a in ma into a long vowel
It turns the t that follows into a d sound
questions.explanation: A small 「っ」 is a one-beat pause that doubles the next consonant, so まって is matte (wait). It is never read as tsu, and it does not change the vowel or voice the consonant.

questions.stem: Which of these is read kitte?
questions.explanation: Only the small 「っ」 gives the doubled t of kitte. A full-size 「つ」 would be read ki-tsu-te, and 「きいて」 is kiite.

questions.stem: How do you read 「ちょっと」?
questions.explanation: 「ちょ」 is cho, the small 「っ」 doubles the t, and 「と」 is to: chotto (a little). There is no 「う」, so the final o is short.

questions.stem: How do you read 「おかあさん」?
questions.explanation: The 「あ」 after 「か」 makes the a long: okaasan, mother. Leaving it short is a common slip, and 「おばあさん」 (obaasan) is grandmother.
「おばあさん」 (obaasan), with a long a, is grandmother. Say the a short and it becomes 「おばさん」 (obasan), aunt, so vowel length really does change the meaning.
The long i in 「おじいさん」 (ojiisan) makes it grandfather. With a short i, 「おじさん」 (ojisan) is uncle.

questions.stem: How do you read 「おおきい」?
questions.explanation: 「おおきい」 (ookii, big) has a long o written with 「お」 and a long i written with 「い」. It is one of the few words that spell a long o with 「お」 rather than 「う」.

questions.stem: In 「せんせい」, how is the final 「せい」 usually pronounced?
options: like se with the e held long
as se followed by a clear i, like say
as a short se, like set
questions.explanation: In everyday speech 「えい」 sounds like a long e, so せんせい sounds like sen-see. It is still spelled with 「い」, and romaji follows the kana: sensei.

questions.stem: In 「おとうさん」, what does the 「う」 after 「と」 do?
options: It doubles the t before it
It shows the word is polite
It makes the o sound long
It adds a separate u sound
questions.explanation: 「う」 after an o sound usually lengthens it: おとうさん is otousan, said with a long o. The politeness comes from 「お」 and 「さん」, not from the 「う」.

questions.stem: Most long o sounds are written with 「う」. Which word writes its long o with 「お」 instead?
questions.explanation: A small group of words write the long o with 「お」: おおきい (ookii, big), とお (too, ten) and おおい (ooi, many). がっこう, ありがとう and おとうさん follow the usual rule with 「う」.

questions.stem: In 「わたしはがくせいです。」, how is 「は」 read?
questions.explanation: As the topic particle, 「は」 is read wa: watashi wa gakusei desu, I am a student. Inside an ordinary word, as in はな (hana), it keeps its sound ha.

questions.stem: In the word 「はな」, how is 「は」 read?
questions.explanation: 「は」 is only read wa when it is the particle. Inside a word it is ha, so はな is hana.

questions.stem: In 「すしをたべます。」, how is 「を」 read?
questions.explanation: 「を」 marks the object and is read o: sushi o tabemasu, I eat sushi. It sounds exactly like 「お」 but is kept for the particle.

questions.stem: In 「がっこうへいきます。」, how is 「へ」 read?
questions.explanation: As the direction particle, 「へ」 is read e: gakkou e ikimasu, I go to school. Inside a word, as in へや (heya, room), it is he.

questions.stem: Which hiragana is used almost only as a particle?
questions.explanation: 「を」 marks the object and almost never appears inside a word. 「は」 and 「へ」 are particles too, but they also spell ordinary words like はな and へや.

questions.stem: How do you read 「こんにちは」?
questions.explanation: The final 「は」 began as the topic particle, so it is read wa. The 「ん」 is a full beat of its own, which is why romaji keeps both n's: konnichiwa.
「さかな」 is sakana, fish. Read it character by character: 「さ」 not 「ち」, and 「な」 not 「ま」.
「ねこ」 is neko, cat. Read it character by character: 「ね」 ends in a loop, which 「れ」 and 「わ」 do not.
「いぬ」 is inu, dog. Read it character by character: 「ぬ」 ends in a loop, which 「め」 does not.

questions.stem: How do you read 「てんぷら」?
questions.explanation: 「てんぷら」 is tenpura, tempura. Read it character by character: the small circle on 「ぷ」 makes it pu, not bu.
「ぶた」 is buta, pig. Read it character by character: two strokes on 「ぶ」 make it bu, where a circle would make it pu.

questions.stem: How do you read 「ありがとう」?
questions.explanation: 「ありがとう」 is arigatou, thank you. Read it character by character: 「が」 has dakuten and the 「う」 lengthens the final o.
「めがね」 is megane, glasses. Read it character by character: 「め」 has no loop and 「ね」 does.

questions.stem: How do you read 「ひらがな」?
questions.explanation: 「ひらがな」 is hiragana, the name of this script. Read it character by character: the script's own name ends in 「な」, not 「ぬ」.
「きっぷ」 is kippu, ticket. Read it character by character: the small 「っ」 doubles the p, and the circle on 「ぷ」 makes it p.

options: simplified cursive forms of whole kanji
small parts cut out of kanji outlines
letters borrowed from the Roman alphabet
Korean letters adapted to write Japanese
questions.explanation: Hiragana grew out of kanji written quickly in a flowing, cursive hand until whole characters became simple shapes. Katakana is the script that came from parts of kanji.

questions.stem: Hiragana 「め」 grew out of a cursive form of which kanji?
questions.explanation: 「め」 comes from 「女」 (woman), written in a flowing hand. 「目」 is the tempting choice because it is also read め (me, eye), but sharing a sound does not make it the source.

questions.stem: In 「食べます」, which job is the hiragana doing?
options: showing how the kanji is pronounced
writing a word borrowed from English
marking the word as especially important
writing the verb ending after the kanji
questions.explanation: The kanji 「食」 carries the meaning eat, and the hiragana 「べます」 writes the ending (tabemasu). Endings written in hiragana after a kanji are called okurigana.

options: kanji that have more than one way to be read
katakana used to spell the names of foreigners
the two small strokes that voice a kana sound
small kana printed with a kanji to show its reading
questions.explanation: Furigana are small kana, usually hiragana, printed above or beside a kanji so a reader who does not know it can still say it. The two small strokes are dakuten.

questions.stem: Which of these is normally written in hiragana?
options: the particles は, を and へ
the name of a foreign country
questions.explanation: Hiragana writes particles, verb and adjective endings, and Japanese words without a common kanji. Foreign names and borrowed words go in katakana.

questions.stem: How many basic hiragana are there, not counting dakuten or small kana?
questions.explanation: There are 46 basic hiragana, from あ to ん. Adding the 25 with dakuten or handakuten gives 71, and 92 is the basic hiragana and katakana together.

questions.stem: Which hiragana stands for a sound with no vowel at all?
questions.explanation: Every basic kana is a vowel or a consonant plus a vowel, except 「ん」 (n). 「し」, 「つ」 and 「す」 all end in a vowel, even when it is said quietly.

questions.stem: How many vowel sounds does Japanese have?
questions.explanation: Japanese has five vowels, a, i, u, e and o, and the chart is built on them: most rows are one consonant joined to each of the five.

questions.stem: How do the sounds of hiragana compare with those of katakana?
options: hiragana sounds are softer than katakana ones
they share shapes but are read differently
the basic sounds are the same, in different shapes
katakana has a separate set of vowel sounds
questions.explanation: 「か」 and 「カ」 are both ka: the two scripts write the same basic sounds with different characters. Katakana adds a few combinations, such as ティ, for sounds in foreign words.
